images.caption: Figure 1:Conceptual comparison of (a) a standard VLA, (b) an illustrative fully connected graph-based VLA, and (c) WeaveVLA. Unlike uniform scene-wide connectivity, WeaveVLA selects task-relevant connections and updates pair-specific relational states across observations.

Figure 2:Architecture of WeaveVLA. Object-level visual features and relative 3D geometry form a task-conditioned relational graph. Graph Transformer blocks encode and propagate relational features, while pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate valid geometric evidence across observations. Cross-attention incorporates vision-language context, and a Q-Former extracts compact relational tokens. The action interface shown is for StarVLA-GR00T.

Figure 3:Real-robot setup and example task trajectories. (a) The dual-arm platform uses a third-person camera for graph construction, a high-mounted main camera, and two wrist cameras. (b) Recorded demonstrations of stacking bowls, placing pens in cups, and cleaning the table. Each row shows four chronological frames from a single demonstration.

Figure 5:Camera-frame geometric errors for absolute
object positions (rose) and relative displacement
vectors (blue), using identical depth predictions
and masks. Left: normalized distributions of signed
depth residuals. Right: depth–lateral residuals
with 50% and 80% density contours.

Figure 6:Qualitative comparison of instance segmentation on LIBERO
(top) and CALVIN scene D (bottom). Columns show RGB observations,
simulator ground-truth masks, and masks produced by the same frozen
SAM 3 model using bounding boxes from the original and fine-tuned
YOLOE detectors. Fine-tuning recovers previously missed instances,
including the plate and cookie box in LIBERO and cabinet components
in CALVIN.
